article.name: CortexDB
article.summary: CortexDB is a Go memory and knowledge-graph library with MCP and gRPC interfaces. Its default storage is a SQLite database that combines scoped memories, knowledge documents/chunks, vectors, full-text indexes, and graph data; PostgreSQL is also supported. The source review is pinned to the verified current main head. No runtime, tests, or benchmarks were run.

who_what.text: The official README describes CortexDB as a local-first Go library for agent memory and a knowledge graph, with MCP and gRPC service integrations plus clients. It is an embeddable library and can also be run behind a shared service; the README advertises a one-file SQLite setup and optional PostgreSQL.

The official GitHub repository identifies main as the default branch. The official main commit feed reports full head 0c6b7b98285a63125328dea95b8fe32f6d182d0d at 2026-11-25T02:41:10Z, and a fresh read-only git ls-remote plus shallow checkout independently resolved main to the same SHA.

architecture.text: The architecture is layered: core storage/indexing and graph engines sit below the public pkg/cortexdb facade; memoryflow and graphflow add ingestion/recall workflows; MCP and gRPC expose tools and APIs. The project overview describes SQLite as the default single-file engine, with vector and FTS indexes alongside graph/RDF data; the README also documents PostgreSQL support.

A memory is a message row addressed by memory_id with content, embedding, bucket/session identifier, role, metadata, importance, TTL and optional evidence grade. Knowledge is a durable record with title/content/source URL/author/collection, metadata, chunks, entities, and timestamps. Ingestion splits documents into chunks and links document, chunk, entity and relation graph records.

The KnowledgeMemory facade composes memory search, knowledge search and graph facts into a context pack. Search paths include lexical retrieval, optional embedding search and graph/PPR routes; the project overview says no-embedder mode remains usable with lexical retrieval.

behavior.text: Memory writes require a nonempty memory_id and content, redact recognized credentials, resolve global/user/session buckets, validate optional evidence grade, embed content when configured, upsert the messages row, mark explicitly superseded IDs, and update the corresponding memory graph node when entities are supplied. UpdateMemory changes content/metadata/importance/TTL and refreshes the vector when content changes.

A memory may be deleted by ID; the implementation removes its message row, cleans an empty bucket, and retracts its graph node so the graph no longer points to a deleted memory. Supersession is a separate explicit mutation: old rows remain stored with superseded_by/superseded_at and are filtered from current recall, while the replacement chain can be returned and queried as of an earlier time.

Knowledge writes preserve source URL, author, metadata, collection, chunks and graph relationships; updates expose partial document fields, expiry and review decisions. The ingestion path uses stable document/chunk identities, content hashes and source fields; re-ingesting changed text retires chunks beyond the new content. Document graph deletion removes source relations and nodes in a transaction and detaches entities still sourced by other documents.

Memory scope resolves to global, user or session buckets plus a namespace. Search filters by the resolved bucket and optional user/session/namespace values; a configured CallerScope can constrain readable/writable buckets. Knowledge collections also carry caller-scope checks. The implementation notes that unconfined library calls remain unchecked, and its scope commentary lists several raw DB/listing/change/chunk-reading paths outside that facade guard; callers should not assume every endpoint is confined by the same predicate.

Recall can combine memories and knowledge, apply minimum evidence grade and as-of filters, and pack bounded context. Memory grades distinguish verified, self_consistent, asserted, held and refused; verified/held/refused require a reason. Graph fact provenance can resolve document IDs, chunk IDs, inferred-rule metadata and supporting text, including reporting source chunk IDs that no longer resolve.

Efficiency and operations mechanisms include FTS and vector indexes, bounded recall/context structures, optional recall explanation, query/result logging that is off unless enabled and has row/age limits, request IDs and trace-context propagation. The inspected source exposes stage and degraded-mode signals; these implementation features do not establish observed speed or resource use.

limits.text: This bounded review inspected the official README and project architecture overview, memory and knowledge APIs, graph document ingestion/deletion, caller-scope commentary, evidence-grade/provenance code, recall explanation/logging and MCP trace middleware. It did not inspect every server adapter, SQL migration, deployment configuration, embedder or graph query path.

Source inspection cannot establish deployed authorization wiring, effective isolation, retrieval accuracy, correction/deletion outcomes, erasure from backups or storage devices, latency, token use, cost, or corpus storage efficiency. No CortexDB runtime, tests, or benchmarks were run.

The project's README and source comments include upstream-reported performance/calibration statements; this review did not reproduce or independently adjudicate those figures, and they are not measurements from this project review.
